word:hebrew:H1111.explanation: Balak is the name of a Moabitish king.

word:hebrew:H1205.explanation: Bᵉʻâthâh means fear. It can also mean trouble.

word:hebrew:H1270.explanation: Barzel means iron. It can also refer to an iron implement, such as a cutting instrument.

word:hebrew:H1353.explanation: Ge'ullah means redemption. It can also refer to the right of redemption.

word:hebrew:H141.explanation: Adoniram is the name of an Israelite.

word:hebrew:H1436.explanation: Gedaljah is a personal name, rendered Gedaliah in English.

word:hebrew:H1524.explanation: Giyl means joy or rejoicing. It can also refer to an age or period of time.

word:hebrew:H1568.explanation: “Gilead” is a proper name for a region east of the Jordan River. In the Old Testament, it identifies a geographical area and can also identify people or groups connected with that region. The name appears 134 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Zechariah. Its uses include descriptions of territory, genealogical references, commands concerning the region, and statements about events associated with it. The surrounding context determines whether Gilead refers specifically to the land or to people identified with it.

word:hebrew:H1582.explanation: Gemalli is a personal name, not a common word describing an object, action, or quality. It identifies one individual in the Hebrew Old Testament and appears only once, in Numbers 13:12. English Bible renderings preserve it as “Gemalli,” treating it as a name rather than translating it into an ordinary meaning phrase. The available lexical information therefore supports recognizing Gemalli as a person’s name, while the surrounding verse is needed to explain that individual’s role in the passage.

word:hebrew:H1667.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to the place name Gath-Rimmon, rendered with the two names “Gath” and “Rimmon.” It functions as a proper name rather than a general description or action. The name occurs eight times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in four verses: three in Joshua and one in 1 Chronicles. Without the surrounding verse text, the word itself identifies the place but does not by itself explain the events or significance associated with it.

word:hebrew:H1689.explanation: Diblah is the name of a place in Syria.

word:hebrew:H1793.explanation: Dakkā means crushed, including the figurative sense of being contrite. It can also refer to destruction.

word:hebrew:H1825.explanation: Dimyôn means resemblance or likeness, as when one thing is described as like another.

word:hebrew:H1850.explanation: Dophkah is the name of a place in the Israelites’ wilderness journey. As a proper name, it identifies a location rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Numbers 33, at Numbers 33:12 and 33:13. The available usage preserves it as “Dophkah,” so its precise name meaning is not established here; its clear function is to identify a place in the journey record.

word:hebrew:H1869.explanation: Darak means to tread. It can also describe going. In another use, it describes bending a bow.

word:hebrew:H1887.explanation: Hê means “behold” or “lo,” calling attention to what follows.

word:hebrew:H1933.explanation: Hava means to be, in the sense of existence.

word:hebrew:H2073.explanation: Zebul means a residence, dwelling, or habitation—a place where someone dwells.

word:hebrew:H2118.explanation: This Hebrew word means “loosed,” describing something being released or allowed to come free. It functions as a verb and appears twice in the Old Testament, both times in Exodus. Its uses are found in Exodus 28:28 and Exodus 39:21, in descriptions involving the priestly garments. The word therefore expresses the action of becoming untied or released, while the surrounding passage identifies what is being loosed and how that action serves the garment’s construction.

word:hebrew:H2154.explanation: Zimmah means a plan, especially a bad one. In context, it can refer to wickedness or a heinous crime.

word:hebrew:H2262.explanation: “Rechabites” is the name of a particular people or family group mentioned in the Hebrew Old Testament. It functions as a proper designation rather than a general description of a person, action, or quality. This Hebrew word occurs once in the Old Testament corpus, at Jeremiah 35:3. The name identifies the group in that passage, while the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain its specific role there.

word:hebrew:H2288.explanation: Chagav means a rift in rocks, a cleft.

word:hebrew:H233.explanation: Azay means at that time, or then.

word:hebrew:H2381.explanation: This Hebrew word is the personal name “Haziel,” identifying one individual rather than describing an action or quality. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 23:9, and the available English renderings preserve it as “Haziel.” Its use here supports understanding it as a proper name, but the supplied material does not establish an additional lexical meaning or explain the person’s role in that verse.

word:hebrew:H2419.explanation: “Hiel” is a personal name, identifying a particular man rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Kings 16:34, so its ordinary function is to identify that individual in the biblical narrative. The name itself should therefore be read as a person’s designation, while the surrounding verse supplies the details about him and what he did. Its rendering remains “Hiel” in the English translations represented here.

word:hebrew:H2420.explanation: Chiydah means a riddle or a difficult saying.

word:hebrew:H2455.explanation: Chol means common, describing what is not set apart as holy. It can also mean profane or unholy, as opposed to what is holy.

word:hebrew:H2532.explanation: Chemdah means delight. It can describe something pleasant, something desired, or something precious.

word:hebrew:H2594.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to “favour”—a gracious benefit or kindness received from someone. It occurs once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jeremiah 16:13, and functions as the object of actions associated with giving and receiving. Its wording presents favor as something that can be granted rather than earned or possessed independently. The surrounding verse determines the precise force of the term there, but its central sense is favor bestowed upon another.

word:hebrew:H2671.explanation: Chêts means an arrow. It can also refer to a wound.

word:hebrew:H2903.explanation: This Hebrew word is rendered “for” in the available English alignment and functions as a small grammatical term within these passages. It occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Exodus 13:16 and Deuteronomy 6:8 and 11:18. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its precise role in each sentence, so its normal meaning here is best stated modestly: it contributes the relationship expressed by “for,” rather than supplying a fuller independent definition.

word:hebrew:H3027.explanation: Yad means hand, especially the open hand. It can also express power, as in Yahweh’s mighty hand, or agency, as when a letter is sent by Uriah’s hand.

word:hebrew:H3085.explanation: “Jehoaddah” is a personal name, referring to a specific man in the Hebrew Old Testament rather than expressing a general idea or action. It appears twice, both times in 1 Chronicles 8:36, within a genealogical record. The surrounding SEE pattern identifies the name with birth or begetting relationships, showing that Jehoaddah is presented as a person within a family line. The available passage evidence does not provide a broader ordinary meaning beyond this name’s identification of that individual.

word:hebrew:H325.explanation: Ahasuerus is a proper name referring to a king. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but the personal designation used for this ruler. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 32 times in 30 verses, chiefly in Esther, with additional occurrences in Ezra and Daniel. The name appears in passages describing the king’s rule, speech, decisions, and commands. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the name Ahasuerus.

word:hebrew:H3276.explanation: Yaal means to profit, be useful, or provide benefit.

word:hebrew:H3342.explanation: Yeqeb means a trough, specifically a winepress or vat where grapes are crushed or their juice drains.

word:hebrew:H3423.explanation: Yarash means to take possession of something, often by driving out its previous occupants. It can also describe inheriting land. In another use, it means disinheriting someone.

word:hebrew:H350.explanation: Ikabod is a personal name. Scripture identifies Ikabod as a son of Phinehas.

word:hebrew:H3526.explanation: Kabas means to wash, including washing garments.

word:hebrew:H3621.explanation: Chelubai is a personal name, rendered “Chelubai.” It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 2:9. The word identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. Its recorded use is connected with a genealogy and a birth or begetting relationship, so its function there is to identify a person within a family record. No broader ordinary meaning is established by this single occurrence.

word:hebrew:H369.explanation: Ayin is a negative particle meaning no or not, and it can mark absence, as when Scripture says there was no water or no king.

word:hebrew:H3759.explanation: Karmel means a planted field, such as a garden, orchard, vineyard, or park. It can also refer by implication to produce from that field, including full ears of grain.

word:hebrew:H3760.explanation: Karmel is the name of a hill in Palestine. It is also the name of a town in Palestine.

word:hebrew:H3856.explanation: This Hebrew word means “was.” It functions as a verb, helping state that someone or something was in a particular condition. In its two Old Testament occurrences, it appears once in Genesis and once in Proverbs, making its recorded use uncommon in the Hebrew corpus. The surrounding words determine the specific condition being stated in each passage; the basic contribution of the word is to express that state as something that was.

word:hebrew:H3922.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to “Lecah,” functioning as a personal or place name rather than describing an action, quality, or object in general. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 4:21, and the available English renderings preserve it as “Lecah.” The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the exact identity associated with the name must be determined from that passage. Its central meaning is therefore the proper name itself: Lecah.

word:hebrew:H3984.explanation: Mâʼn means a utensil or vessel.

word:hebrew:H400.explanation: Okel means food—something gathered or bought to eat.

word:hebrew:H4123.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to “deceits,” naming things that mislead rather than express what is true. It functions as a noun for deceptive matters, not as an action or command. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 30:10. Its basic sense remains focused on deceit itself; the surrounding verse determines the specific force intended in that occurrence.

word:hebrew:H4215.explanation: Mezareh means a scatterer, associated here with the north wind.

word:hebrew:H4260.explanation: Machămâ’âh means something buttery, unctuous, and pleasant. Figuratively, it can describe flattering words that sound smooth while concealing hostility.

word:hebrew:H4321.explanation: Mikajah is a personal name, rendered Micaiah in English Scripture.

word:hebrew:H439.explanation: “Allon” is a Hebrew proper name, used to identify a particular named referent rather than to describe a general action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both within Genesis 35:8, so it is a rare name with a very limited scriptural occurrence. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

word:hebrew:H4585.explanation: Meonah means a dwelling place or refuge. It can also mean a den where animals take cover.

word:hebrew:H475.explanation: Eliashib is a personal name used for Israelites.

word:hebrew:H4776.explanation: This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezra 4:19. Because the verse text and a clear English rendering are not available here, the safest reading is to treat it as a context-bound term rather than assign it a broader meaning. The reference identifies its location, but not its meaning by itself. Its precise force must be determined from the surrounding passage.

word:hebrew:H4808.explanation: Meribah means quarrel. The name is associated with strife at the waters and with provocation in the wilderness.

word:hebrew:H4901.explanation: Meshek means a sowing. It can also describe something precious. In another use, it means a price.

word:hebrew:H4996.explanation: No is a place name for Thebes, the capital of Upper Egypt.

word:hebrew:H5083.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to “gifts”—things given to another person. Its recorded use presents it as the object of giving, so the word focuses on what is handed over rather than on the giver or recipient. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezekiel 16:33. Its associated scriptural pattern is giving, reinforcing the sense of gifts offered or transferred to someone else.

word:hebrew:H5102.explanation: Nahar means to flow together or assemble. It can also mean to be lightened.

word:hebrew:H5209.explanation: Nîyn means progeny. It is rendered as “son” when referring to a family descendant.

word:hebrew:H5230.explanation: Nakal means to defraud or act treacherously.

word:hebrew:H5245.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to a “leopard,” the name of an animal. It functions as a direct animal term, not as a description of an action or quality. In the Hebrew corpus represented here, it appears once, in Daniel 7:6. The word therefore carries a narrow, concrete meaning rather than a broad abstract idea. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:hebrew:H5313.explanation: Niphqa means an outgo or expense.

word:hebrew:H552.explanation: Umnam means indeed or in very deed. It can also mean “of a surety,” expressing certainty.

word:hebrew:H5591.explanation: Saar means a hurricane, storm, tempest, or whirlwind.

word:hebrew:H5634.explanation: Sarappah means a twig or bough.

word:hebrew:H5678.explanation: ʻEbrâh means an outburst of passion. It can appear as anger, rage, or wrath.

word:hebrew:H5692.explanation: Uggah means a cake. It can describe a round ashcake baked on a hearth.

word:hebrew:H5872.explanation: En-Gedi is the name of a place.

word:hebrew:H5898.explanation: This Hebrew name refers to Salt City, a place named in the Old Testament. Its meaning is indicated by “Salt,” while “cities” reflects how the place name appears in the English rendering. The name occurs twice in one verse, Joshua 15:62, within a list of places. Without the verse text or wider setting, the name itself gives the clearest meaning: a city or settlement identified with salt.

word:hebrew:H5937.explanation: Alaz means to jump for joy—to exult, rejoice, or triumph.

word:hebrew:H5995.explanation: Amir means a bunch of grain. It can describe a handful after harvesting. It can also refer to a sheaf.

word:hebrew:H6033.explanation: This Hebrew word means “poor,” describing a person with little material wealth or resources. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Daniel 4:27, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse rather than repeated biblical usage. As a descriptive word, it identifies a person’s low economic condition. The available English renderings consistently use “poor,” supporting this central meaning without establishing additional meanings.

word:hebrew:H6125.explanation: Aqah means constraint, and this occurrence is rendered as oppression.

word:hebrew:H6150.explanation: This Hebrew word means “darkened,” describing a condition in which something loses its light or brightness. It occurs three times in the Old Testament, functioning as a predicate that describes what happens to a subject. Its recorded use includes Judges 19:9, 1 Samuel 17:16, and Isaiah 24:11. The exact force in each verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is the state or action of becoming darkened rather than a person, object, or place by itself.

word:hebrew:H6169.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to “paper,” functioning as a noun for that material. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Isaiah 19:7. Its normal lexical sense is therefore narrow and concrete rather than a broad description of an action, quality, or person. The surrounding verse determines how the noun functions in that specific passage, but the word itself identifies paper.

word:hebrew:H6187.explanation: Erek means an estimation or valuation. In the law, it could refer to a stated amount in silver, while a priest assigned a value according to a person's ability to pay.

word:hebrew:H6204.explanation: Orpah is a personal name. It identifies one of the two Moabite women who married into Naomi’s family. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this name occurs twice, both times in Ruth 1. Because it functions as a person’s name rather than a common descriptive word, its ordinary meaning here is identification: Orpah. The name appears in Ruth 1:4 and Ruth 1:14.

word:hebrew:H6341.explanation: Pach means a thin sheet of metal. It can also refer to a snare.

word:hebrew:H6446.explanation: Pas means a tunic. It can also refer to a garment of many or varied colors.

word:hebrew:H646.explanation: The word refers to an “ephod,” a named object associated with priestly service and worship. In the Old Testament, it occurs 49 times, especially in passages concerning the tabernacle, priests, and Israel’s worship. It is also mentioned in accounts involving Samuel’s service and David’s actions. The word normally functions as the name of this sacred item, while the surrounding passage clarifies its particular use. Scripture connects it with commanded workmanship, priestly service, and carrying or handling the object.

word:hebrew:H6547.explanation: Paroh means Pharaoh, a general title for Egyptian kings.

word:hebrew:H66.explanation: Abel-Majim is the name of a place in Palestine.

word:hebrew:H6600.explanation: Pithgam refers to a word, an answer, a letter, a matter, or a decree.

word:hebrew:H6639.explanation: The Hebrew word means “swell,” describing something becoming enlarged or rising in size. It functions as a verb, expressing an increase rather than naming an object or person. In its Hebrew Bible usage, it occurs once, at Numbers 5:21. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic idea is physical swelling or becoming enlarged. This is a specific action word describing a change in size.

word:hebrew:H6675.explanation: Tso’ah means excrement or dung, and can also describe filth.

word:hebrew:H6811.explanation: Tsair is a place in Idumaea, known in the English text as Zair.

word:hebrew:H6886.explanation: Tsarephath is a place in Palestine, called Zarephath in English.

word:hebrew:H7001.explanation: Qetar means a knot or, figuratively, a riddle. In another sense, it refers to a vertebra or joint.

word:hebrew:H7096.explanation: Qatsah means to cut off. It can also describe scraping something off. Figuratively, it can mean to destroy.

word:hebrew:H7108.explanation: This Hebrew word describes someone as “furious.” It functions as a descriptive word, presenting a person’s sharply aroused anger rather than a calm or moderate response. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in Daniel 2:12, and the available English renderings agree on “furious.” Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, this cache explains the word’s normal lexical sense, while the precise force of the word in Daniel 2:12 belongs to the passage itself.

word:hebrew:H7210.explanation: Ro'i means sight or vision. It can also mean a spectacle.

word:hebrew:H7229.explanation: Rab means great. It can also refer to a human authority, such as a lord or a captain.

word:hebrew:H7265.explanation: Regaz means to provoke to wrath.

word:hebrew:H747.explanation: Arisai is a personal name, identifying an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, and its English rendering remains “Arisai.” The word appears in Esther 9:9, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain that passage’s specific context. As a name, its main function is to identify the person mentioned in the account, not to provide a broader definition or instruction.

word:hebrew:H7522.explanation: Ratsown means delight, favor, or what is acceptable. It can also refer to willing choice, desire, or pleasure.

word:hebrew:H7584.explanation: Shaavah means a rushing tempest and can also mean desolation.

word:hebrew:H7614.explanation: Sheba is a personal name. It is also used as the name of a place associated with a queen.

word:hebrew:H7658.explanation: “Seven” is the meaning of this Hebrew word. It functions as a number, identifying a quantity of seven. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Job 42:13. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its specific role in that sentence cannot be described beyond its basic numerical meaning. Its central sense remains a precise count of seven.

word:hebrew:H7777.explanation: Shual is a Hebrew word preserved in English as the name “Shual,” rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive term. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, with one occurrence in 1 Samuel and one in 1 Chronicles. The same rendering appears in both places, so its consistent use is best understood as a proper name or designation. The precise reference of the name depends on the surrounding verse context, which is not included here.

word:hebrew:H7799.explanation: Shushan means lily, a flower. It can also refer to lily work used as architectural ornament.

word:hebrew:H7823.explanation: Shachis means after-growth, that which springs up from what grew of itself.

word:hebrew:H790.explanation: Eshban is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Eshban” in English. It does not have an explicit definition in the available lexical information, so its significance is as a name rather than as a translated descriptive word. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice: in Genesis 36:26 and 1 Chronicles 1:41. Both occurrences preserve the same English rendering, “Eshban,” confirming that the word functions consistently as a proper name.

word:hebrew:H7926.explanation: Shekem means the shoulder, a place where burdens are carried.

word:hebrew:H8071.explanation: Simlah means a garment or item of clothing, especially a mantle. It can serve as a covering for the skin.

word:hebrew:H8219.explanation: Shephelah means lowland, a low plain or vale.

word:hebrew:H8255.explanation: Sheqel refers to a weight used as a commercial standard. It appears in amounts of silver, such as land valued at four hundred shekels and a half-shekel offering.

word:hebrew:H8332.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to “banishment,” the removal of a person from the community. It names an imposed separation rather than an ordinary departure. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both within Ezra 7:26, so its recorded use is limited to that passage. The precise force in the verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense is exclusion through banishment.

word:hebrew:H8462.explanation: Tᵉchillâh means beginning or commencement. It can also mean first, including a first occasion.

word:hebrew:H8488.explanation: Temeni is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Temeni.” It identifies an individual rather than expressing a general action, quality, or object. The name occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 4:6. Its recorded setting is a genealogy, so its main function is to identify a person within a family record. No broader lexical meaning is established here beyond the name itself.

word:hebrew:H8516.explanation: Talbosheth means a garment or clothing.

word:hebrew:H8581.explanation: Ta'ab means to loathe or morally detest.

word:hebrew:H8673.explanation: This Hebrew word means “ninety,” the numerical value used when Scripture gives a count or number. It functions as a number rather than naming a person, place, object, or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 20 times across 20 verses, from Genesis through Daniel. Its precise significance in any individual verse depends on the surrounding statement, but its basic meaning remains the number ninety.

word:hebrew:H905.explanation: Bad means alone or apart. It can also mean only. In another use, it means beside or besides.

word:hebrew:H949.explanation: Botsets is the name of a rock, rendered Bozez in English.

word:hebrew:H970.explanation: Bachur means a young man or youth. It can also describe someone chosen.
